title: What the Clumps Said
paragraphs: In 1667 a Paris physician, Jean-Baptiste Denis, ran lamb's blood into the veins of a feverish boy, who lived; a later patient died, and within a few years France forbade transfusion.
The practice returned in 1818, when the London obstetrician James Blundell began moving blood from one person into another, often to rescue women bleeding after childbirth.
Some patients rallied; others grew feverish, passed dark urine, and died, and no one could say why the same procedure saved one and killed the next.
The answer came in 1901, from Vienna, through an experiment simple enough to repeat on a glass slide.
Karl Landsteiner drew blood from himself and a handful of colleagues, separated the fluid serum from the red cells, and mixed each person's serum with each person's cells.
Some mixtures stayed smooth and others clumped, and the samples sorted into three groups, which Landsteiner called A, B, and C; group C, whose cells clumped with no one's serum, was later renamed O.
A fourth group, AB, turned up the following year when two of his colleagues tested more people.
Landsteiner received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for the discovery in 1930.
Red cells carry molecular markers called antigens; in the ABO system these are short chains of sugars, and a cell may display the A sugar, the B sugar, both, or neither.

Plasma carries antibodies, proteins that bind to antigens the body treats as foreign, and the pattern is a mirror image: A cells come with anti-B, B cells with anti-A, AB cells with neither, and O cells with both.
Because an antibody has more than one binding arm, it can bridge neighboring cells into a lattice, and that lattice is agglutination, the clumping Landsteiner saw.

Curiously, these antibodies appear in the first months of life with no transfusion to provoke them, probably because common gut bacteria carry similar sugars and the infant's immune system learns its targets from them.
The rule for safe transfusion follows directly: a recipient's plasma must contain no antibody against the donor's cells.
Group O cells, carrying neither sugar, can therefore go to anyone, and a group AB recipient, carrying neither antibody, can accept cells of any group.
Break the rule and the donor's cells are agglutinated and then torn open inside the recipient's vessels, spilling hemoglobin into the plasma.
The patient develops fever, chills, back pain, and dark urine; the free hemoglobin can injure the kidneys, and a large mismatch can kill within hours.
This is almost certainly what Blundell was seeing.

I would add one caution about the phrase 'universal donor': it is true of O cells but not of O plasma, which is loaded with anti-A and anti-B, and the phrase has encouraged more confidence than it deserves.
Knowing the groups did not make transfusion practical, because blood begins to clot the moment it leaves the body.
For more than a decade afterward, surgeons still had to connect donor to recipient directly, sometimes artery to vein, with no way to measure how much blood had passed.
The remedy was chemical.
Clotting depends on calcium ions at several steps, and sodium citrate binds calcium, so a small amount of citrate added to freshly drawn blood keeps it liquid.

Between 1914 and 1915 the idea was put to work independently by Albert Hustin in Brussels, Luis Agote in Buenos Aires, and Richard Lewisohn in New York, who found a dose low enough to be safe and high enough to stop clotting.
By 1917 Oswald Robertson, an American physician serving with the British, was keeping bottles of citrated blood on ice for the wounded of the Western Front.
Once blood could wait, it could be stockpiled.

In 1937 Bernard Fantus, a physician at Cook County Hospital in Chicago, opened a laboratory where donated blood was typed, citrated, and refrigerated against future need, and he gave it the name that stuck: a blood bank.
The metaphor was deliberate: families deposited blood that the patient could later withdraw, and the idea spread quickly to hospitals across the United States.
The ABO groups explained most transfusion disasters but not all of them.

In 1939 Philip Levine and Rufus Stetson described a woman who, after a stillbirth, reacted violently to blood from her husband that matched her ABO group; her serum clumped his cells, pointing to an antigen outside the ABO system.
The following year Landsteiner, by then at the Rockefeller Institute in New York, and Alexander Wiener injected red cells from rhesus monkeys into rabbits and guinea pigs.

Their antiserum clumped the red cells of about 85 percent of the New Yorkers tested, and the two men named the factor Rh, after the monkey; people whose cells reacted were Rh positive, the rest Rh negative.

The name has outlived its accuracy: the rabbit antibody and the human antibody turned out to recognize different molecules, and the rabbit target is now called LW, for Landsteiner and Wiener, while the human antigen keeps the name Rh.
The Rh factor mattered less for transfusion, where it could simply be matched, than for pregnancy.
An Rh negative woman carrying an Rh positive fetus is usually safe in that first pregnancy, because fetal red cells enter her circulation mainly at delivery.

Once they do, she can form anti-Rh antibodies, and in a later pregnancy those antibodies cross the placenta and destroy the red cells of an Rh positive fetus, causing hemolytic disease of the newborn.
Levine connected the disease to the Rh factor in 1941.

The prevention, introduced in the late 1960s, is elegant: an Rh negative mother receives ready-made anti-Rh antibody shortly after delivery, which clears the fetal cells from her blood before her own immune system notices them.
Where it is used, a disease that once commonly killed infants has become rare, and I count it among the cleanest victories of preventive medicine.
Storing blood for a hospital is one problem; moving it across an ocean in wartime is another, and Charles Drew solved the second.

Drew, a surgeon whose 1940 doctoral dissertation at Columbia University was titled Banked Blood, was asked that year to supervise Blood for Britain, which collected blood in New York and shipped it to a country under bombardment.
He chose to ship plasma rather than whole blood.

Plasma restores blood volume, which is what a bleeding soldier most needs; it keeps longer than red cells; and plasma pooled from many donors can be given with less regard to group, since any one donor's antibodies are diluted.
Drew also pushed the drying of plasma to a powder that could travel without refrigeration and be reconstituted with sterile water near the front.
In 1941 he became the first director of the American Red Cross blood bank in New York and sent out the mobile collection units that today's blood drives descend from.
The program's rules were less rational than its chemistry.
The Red Cross, at the request of the armed forces, at first refused blood from Black donors, and when the policy changed in 1942 it accepted that blood only if it was stored and labeled separately.

Drew, who was Black, had by then returned to Howard University to teach surgery, and he said plainly that the practice had no basis in science, since nothing in the plasma marks the race of the donor.
He died in 1950 after a car accident in North Carolina, at the age of forty five.
It is hard to read this episode without anger: the decade that produced the Rh test and the dried-plasma bottle also produced a labeling rule that the science of the labels flatly contradicted.
Landsteiner's experiment is, in the end, a lesson in which questions to ask.
He did not ask why transfusion sometimes killed; he asked whether blood from different people behaved differently in a dish, and the dish answered in clumps.
Every advance that followed had the same shape, a rule read off the blood and then a tool that put it to use: the citrate bottle, the bank, the Rh test, the plasma shipment.
Where the story went wrong, it went wrong by adding a category that the blood did not contain.

questions.stem: According to the passage, James Blundell's transfusions in the early nineteenth century
choices: were forbidden in France within a few years of his first attempt
used the blood of lambs when human donors could not be found
saved some patients and killed others for reasons no one could explain
were performed mainly on soldiers wounded on the battlefield
were abandoned once their patients' fevers and dark urine were traced to lamb's blood

proof.quote: no one could say why the same procedure saved one and killed the next

questions.why: Paragraph 1 says some of Blundell's patients rallied while others grew feverish and died, and no one could say why the same procedure saved one and killed the next.
distractorNotes: Wrong person: the ban in France followed Denis's work in the 1660s, not Blundell's.
Wrong person: lamb's blood belongs to Denis in 1667; Blundell moved blood from one person into another.
Outside the passage: paragraph 1 says he often treated women bleeding after childbirth, not soldiers.
Outside the passage: nothing says the practice was abandoned, and lamb's blood had nothing to do with Blundell's patients.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Landsteiner identified the blood groups by
choices: mixing the serum of each person with the red cells of each other person
injecting red cells from monkeys into rabbits and guinea pigs
adding sodium citrate to freshly drawn blood and watching it clot
testing a larger set of people the year after his first paper appeared
comparing the blood of patients who survived transfusion with those who died

proof.quote: mixed each person's serum with each person's cells

questions.why: Paragraph 2 describes the experiment: Landsteiner separated serum from red cells and mixed each person's serum with each person's cells, and the clumping sorted the samples into groups.
distractorNotes: Wrong paragraph: the monkey experiment is the Rh work of 1940 in paragraph 7.
Wrong paragraph and reversed: citrate in paragraph 5 stops clotting, and it came more than a decade later.
Wrong people: paragraph 2 says two of his colleagues tested more people the following year and found AB.
Outside the passage: Landsteiner mixed blood from healthy colleagues, not from transfusion patients.

questions.stem: The author mentions gut bacteria in paragraph 3 primarily to
choices: warn that infections can trigger a dangerous transfusion reaction
explain why infants are unable to receive transfusions safely
argue that the ABO antigens originally evolved in bacteria
show that antibodies against blood sugars require a prior transfusion
account for antibodies that form without any transfusion

proof.quote: these antibodies appear in the first months of life with no transfusion to provoke them, probably because common gut bacteria carry similar sugars

questions.why: Paragraph 3 calls it curious that the antibodies appear with no transfusion to provoke them, then offers gut bacteria with similar sugars as the probable explanation.
distractorNotes: Outside the passage: nothing links infection to transfusion reactions.
Outside the passage: the passage says nothing about transfusing infants.
Too strong: the passage says the bacteria carry similar sugars, not that the antigens evolved in them.
Reversed: the whole point is that these antibodies form without any transfusion.

questions.stem: According to the passage, a person whose red cells carry the B sugar has plasma that contains
choices: anti-B only
anti-A only
both anti-A and anti-B
neither anti-A nor anti-B
anti-A until the first months of life, then neither

proof.quote: B cells with anti-A

questions.why: Paragraph 3 gives the mirror-image pattern: A cells come with anti-B, B cells with anti-A, AB cells with neither, and O cells with both.
distractorNotes: Reversed: anti-B belongs to a person with A cells, and a person's plasma never attacks the sugar their own cells carry.
Wrong group: both antibodies belong to a person with O cells.
Wrong group: neither antibody belongs to a person with AB cells.
Reversed timing: paragraph 3 says the antibodies appear in the first months of life, not that they disappear then.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that if a patient with group A blood were given group B red cells, the most likely result would be that
choices: the recipient's cells would be agglutinated by the donor's anti-A
the donor's cells would be accepted because the A and B sugars are nearly identical
the recipient's immune system would need several months to form anti-B
the recipient's anti-B would clump the donor's cells and tear them open
the recipient would form anti-B only after a second transfusion

proof.quote: A cells come with anti-B
a recipient's plasma must contain no antibody against the donor's cells
the donor's cells are agglutinated and then torn open inside the recipient's vessels

questions.why: Paragraph 3 says a person with A cells already carries anti-B, and paragraph 4 says that when the rule is broken the donor's cells are agglutinated and then torn open. Put those together and the recipient's anti-B attacks the incoming B cells.
distractorNotes: Reversed direction: red cells were given, not plasma, and paragraph 4 says it is the donor's cells that are attacked.
Contradicted: paragraph 3 treats A and B as different sugars with different antibodies against them.
Wrong timing: paragraph 3 says the antibodies are already present from the first months of life.
Wrong timing: anti-B is already there in group A plasma, so no first transfusion is needed to create it.

questions.stem: As used in paragraph 4, the word 'loaded' most nearly means
choices: filled with
weighed down by
armed with
biased toward
wealthy from

proof.quote: O plasma, which is loaded with anti-A and anti-B

questions.why: Paragraph 4 says O plasma is loaded with anti-A and anti-B, and the point is that the plasma holds plenty of both antibodies. Loaded here means full of.
distractorNotes: Burdened is a common sense of loaded, but the sentence is about what the plasma contains, not about a weight it carries.
A loaded gun is armed, but plasma is not a weapon being readied.
A loaded question is biased, but the sentence describes contents, not a slant.
Loaded can mean rich, but nothing in the sentence concerns money.

questions.stem: According to the passage, all of the following are true of sodium citrate EXCEPT:
choices: It binds calcium ions.
It keeps freshly drawn blood liquid.
It was first used in transfusion by Oswald Robertson.
It was put to work independently by researchers in Brussels, Buenos Aires, and New York.
Its safe dose was worked out by Richard Lewisohn.

proof.quote: sodium citrate binds calcium
keeps it liquid
put to work independently by Albert Hustin in Brussels, Luis Agote in Buenos Aires, and Richard Lewisohn in New York
who found a dose low enough to be safe and high enough to stop clotting
By 1917 Oswald Robertson, an American physician serving with the British, was keeping bottles of citrated blood on ice

questions.why: Paragraph 5 credits Hustin, Agote, and Lewisohn with putting citrate to work between 1914 and 1915. Robertson appears later, by 1917, storing bottles of citrated blood on ice; he did not introduce it.
distractorNotes: Stated in paragraph 5: sodium citrate binds calcium.
Stated in paragraph 5: a small amount of citrate keeps freshly drawn blood liquid.
Stated in paragraph 5, which names the three men and their three cities.
Stated in paragraph 5: Lewisohn found a dose low enough to be safe and high enough to stop clotting.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Bernard Fantus
choices: coined the term 'blood bank' to describe a program for shipping plasma overseas
first demonstrated that citrated blood could be kept on ice for the wounded
opened the first blood bank at the Rockefeller Institute in New York
discovered that donated blood could be refrigerated for only a few days
opened a Chicago laboratory where blood was typed, citrated, and stored

proof.quote: opened a laboratory where donated blood was typed, citrated, and refrigerated against future need

questions.why: Paragraph 6 says Fantus, at Cook County Hospital in Chicago, opened a laboratory where donated blood was typed, citrated, and refrigerated against future need, and named it a blood bank.
distractorNotes: Mash-up: Fantus did coin the term, but the plasma shipments belong to Drew in paragraph 9.
Wrong person: paragraph 5 credits Oswald Robertson with keeping citrated blood on ice for the wounded.
Wrong place: paragraph 6 puts the bank at Cook County Hospital in Chicago; the Rockefeller Institute is where Landsteiner worked.
Outside the passage: no storage limit is given for Fantus's bank.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that adding calcium to a bottle of citrated blood would most likely
choices: tear the red cells open
let the blood begin to clot once again
make the blood safe for a recipient of any group
extend the time the blood could be stored on ice
lower the dose of citrate needed to keep the blood liquid

proof.quote: Clotting depends on calcium ions at several steps, and sodium citrate binds calcium

questions.why: Paragraph 5 says clotting depends on calcium ions and that citrate works by binding calcium. Supplying calcium again would undo that and let the blood clot.
distractorNotes: Wrong mechanism: in paragraph 4 cells are torn open by an antibody mismatch, not by calcium.
Unrelated: group compatibility in paragraph 4 depends on sugars and antibodies, not on calcium.
Reversed: restoring clotting would ruin the bottle, not preserve it longer.
Reversed: more calcium would call for more citrate to bind it, not less.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the Rh factor got its name from
choices: the woman whose serum first revealed an antigen outside the ABO system
the two researchers who identified it, Landsteiner and Wiener
the Rockefeller Institute, where the experiment was carried out
the rhesus monkeys whose red cells were used to produce the antiserum
the roughly 85 percent of New Yorkers whose cells reacted to the antiserum

proof.quote: named the factor Rh, after the monkey

questions.why: Paragraph 7 says Landsteiner and Wiener injected red cells from rhesus monkeys into rabbits and guinea pigs and named the factor Rh, after the monkey.
distractorNotes: Wrong detail: the Levine and Stetson patient pointed to the antigen but gave it no name.
Wrong name: paragraph 7 says the researchers' initials went to LW, the rabbit target, not to Rh.
Outside the passage: the institute is where Landsteiner worked, not the source of the name.
Wrong detail: the 85 percent figure describes how many people were Rh positive, not where the name came from.

questions.stem: The author mentions the LW antigen in paragraph 7 primarily to
choices: credit Landsteiner and Wiener for a second discovery as important as the first
argue that the Rh test should be replaced by a more accurate one
note that the Rh name no longer matches what the original antibody detected
explain why about 85 percent of people tested were Rh positive
show that the human antibody and the rabbit antibody are identical

proof.quote: The name has outlived its accuracy

questions.why: Paragraph 7 introduces LW with the words 'the name has outlived its accuracy': the rabbit antibody and the human antibody turned out to recognize different molecules, so the name Rh stuck to an antigen the original experiment did not actually detect.
distractorNotes: Too strong: the sentence is about a mismatch in naming, not a second major discovery.
Outside the passage: the author never questions the test, only the name.
Wrong detail: the 85 percent figure comes from the antiserum result, and LW does not explain it.
Reversed: paragraph 7 says the two antibodies recognize different molecules.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that an Rh positive woman carrying an Rh negative fetus would most likely
choices: form no anti-Rh antibodies against the fetal cells
need ready-made anti-Rh antibody after delivery
form anti-Rh antibodies at delivery, as an Rh negative woman would
deliver a child with hemolytic disease of the newborn
be unharmed only until a second pregnancy

proof.quote: An Rh negative woman carrying an Rh positive fetus
Once they do, she can form anti-Rh antibodies
proteins that bind to antigens the body treats as foreign

questions.why: Paragraph 8 builds the danger on an Rh negative mother meeting Rh positive fetal cells, and paragraph 3 says antibodies form against antigens the body treats as foreign. Flip the pairing and the fetal cells carry no Rh antigen for her to react to, so no anti-Rh forms.
distractorNotes: Reversed: paragraph 8 gives the ready-made antibody to Rh negative mothers, who are the ones at risk of forming their own.
Reversed: the antibody forms in a mother who lacks the antigen her fetus carries; here the fetus lacks it.
Reversed: paragraph 8 ties the disease to anti-Rh antibodies destroying an Rh positive fetus's cells.
Reversed: the second-pregnancy risk in paragraph 8 belongs to the Rh negative mother.

questions.stem: A patient with group B blood needs red cells, and the hospital has cells of only one group on hand. According to the rule in paragraph 4, which of the following supplies could be given safely?
choices: group A cells, because the recipient's plasma carries only anti-A
group AB cells, because they carry both sugars and so match any recipient
group A or AB cells, because the recipient's anti-A is diluted by the donor's plasma
group O cells, because they carry neither sugar for the recipient's anti-A to bind
cells of any group, because the recipient's antibodies attack only foreign plasma

proof.quote: a recipient's plasma must contain no antibody against the donor's cells
Group O cells, carrying neither sugar, can therefore go to anyone
B cells with anti-A

questions.why: Paragraph 3 says a group B person carries anti-A, and paragraph 4's rule is that the recipient's plasma must hold no antibody against the donor's cells. Group O cells carry neither sugar, so there is nothing for the anti-A to bind.
distractorNotes: Reversed: carrying anti-A is exactly why group A cells would be agglutinated.
Reversed: AB cells carry the A sugar, which the recipient's anti-A attacks; carrying both sugars makes AB a universal recipient, not a universal donor.
Wrong mechanism: dilution of antibodies in paragraph 9 concerns pooled plasma, and the recipient's own anti-A is not diluted by a transfusion of cells.
Contradicted: paragraph 4 says antibodies attack the donor's cells, not plasma.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Drew chose to ship plasma rather than whole blood partly because plasma
choices: carries the red cells that a bleeding soldier most urgently needs
could be shipped only after being dried to a powder
can be stored for weeks without any refrigeration
contains no antibodies against the ABO sugars
keeps longer than red cells and restores blood volume

proof.quote: it keeps longer than red cells

questions.why: Paragraph 9 lists three reasons: plasma restores blood volume, it keeps longer than red cells, and pooled plasma dilutes any one donor's antibodies.
distractorNotes: Contradicted: plasma is what remains without the red cells; paragraph 9 says what a bleeding soldier most needs is blood volume.
Too strong: paragraph 9 presents drying as an additional technique Drew pushed, not a requirement for shipping.
Half right: paragraph 9 says the dried powder travels without refrigeration, not plasma in general.
Contradicted: paragraph 9 says pooling dilutes the donors' antibodies, which means plasma still contains them.

questions.stem: According to the passage, each of the following is true of Charles Drew EXCEPT:
choices: He wrote a doctoral dissertation titled Banked Blood.
He resigned from the Red Cross in protest at its donor policy.
He directed the first American Red Cross blood bank in New York.
He died at forty five after a car accident in North Carolina.
He said that separating blood by race had no basis in science.

proof.quote: doctoral dissertation at Columbia University was titled Banked Blood
the first director of the American Red Cross blood bank in New York
He died in 1950 after a car accident in North Carolina, at the age of forty five
the practice had no basis in science
had by then returned to Howard University to teach surgery

questions.why: Paragraph 10 says Drew had already returned to Howard University by the time the policy changed, and it never says he resigned in protest. The other four statements appear in paragraphs 9 and 10.
distractorNotes: Stated in paragraph 9: his 1940 doctoral dissertation at Columbia was titled Banked Blood.
Stated in paragraph 9: in 1941 he became the first director of the American Red Cross blood bank in New York.
Stated in paragraph 10: he died in 1950 after a car accident in North Carolina, at forty five.
Stated in paragraph 10: he said plainly that the practice had no basis in science.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the policy of labeling blood by the donor's race is best described as
choices: amused
neutral
indignant
ambivalent
resigned

proof.quote: It is hard to read this episode without anger
The program's rules were less rational than its chemistry.

questions.why: Paragraph 10 opens by calling the rules less rational than the chemistry and closes with 'It is hard to read this episode without anger.' That is indignation, a controlled anger at something unjust.
distractorNotes: Wrong register: nothing in paragraph 10 is treated as funny.
Too weak: the author states anger openly rather than withholding judgment.
Too weak: the author takes one clear side; there is no wavering between two views.
Wrong register: resignation accepts a wrong quietly, and this author calls it out.

questions.stem: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
choices: Karl Landsteiner's 1930 Nobel Prize was the most important award ever given for research on human blood.
Safe transfusion grew from rules read off the blood itself, each put to use by a practical tool.
Charles Drew's plasma program proved that whole blood should never be shipped in wartime.
The Rh factor, not the ABO system, explains most of the deaths from early transfusion.
Blood banking succeeded in the United States because families were willing to deposit blood.

proof.quote: a rule read off the blood and then a tool that put it to use
Landsteiner's experiment is, in the end, a lesson in which questions to ask
The rule for safe transfusion follows directly

questions.why: The passage moves from Landsteiner's clumps to the citrate bottle, the bank, the Rh test, and the plasma shipment, and paragraph 11 names the pattern: a rule read off the blood and then a tool that put it to use.
distractorNotes: Too extreme and never said: the Nobel Prize is a one-sentence detail in paragraph 2.
Too extreme: paragraph 9 gives Drew's reasons for plasma, but never says whole blood should never be shipped.
Reversed: paragraph 7 says the ABO groups explained most transfusion disasters, and Rh the rest.
A detail: the deposit idea is one sentence in paragraph 6, not the passage's point.
